newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serb leader urges people in last enclave to vote.
newsitem.headline: Serb leader urges people in last enclave to vote.

text.p: Serbs from the Eastern Slavonia enclave, due to revert to Croatian rule soon, stressed on Wednesday their participation and victory in crucial elections in the enclave was indispensable for their survival there.

Their leader Vojislav Stanimirovic urged all the people to obtain Croatian citizenship papers, which would qualify them for the first postwar voting in the enclave, held on Sunday, simultaneously with regional and local polls in Croatia.

"We call on the residents to get their documents until Saturday... so we could gain an absolute majority in the cities and municipalites," Stanimirovic said after talks with the U.N. administrator of the region, U.S. general Jacques Klein.

Serbs in the fertile, oil-producing Eastern Slavonia rebelled against Croatia's independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991 and carved out their own state, loosely linked with two other rebel enclaves.
But Zagreb recaptured the other two and agreed to peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia, now monitored by some 5,000 U.N. peacekeepers (UNTAES), whose mandate expires on July 15.
Croatian document offices started issuing documents to the Serbs in the enclave last year, but not all the Serbs have applied.
Zagreb wants to hold the election and "reintegrate" the enclave as soon as possible so it can start returning over 80,000 refugees who were expelled by the Serbs in 1991.

"With or without us, the elections are going to be held," said Stanimirovic's statement, faxed to Reuters. "The only way and only chance for us to keep on existing here is if the Serbs make up an absolute majority," he said.

The statement apparently overruled recent hints made by the Regional Assembly, a relic of old rebel administration with no real power, that the Serbs, dissatisfied with the conditions of voting, could boycott the poll.

Of some 120,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia now, about half are refugees from other enclaves. At least a quarter of them are expected to flee rather than wait for the pending restoration of Croatia's rule.

Some 68,000 Croat refugees are eligible to vote on Sunday, against roughly 73,000 Serb voters, whose number may still increase before Sunday, in line with UNTAES's efforts to ecourage people to vote by extending deadlines for their registration.
